purpose: Alcohol antiseptic is used to kill germs, bacteria, and some viruses on your skin to help prevent the spread of infection. It is commonly used to clean hands when soap and water are not available, or to clean small areas of skin before an injection or medical procedure. It is an important tool for everyday hygiene and infection prevention.
how_it_works: Alcohol works by breaking down the outer coating of germs and bacteria, which destroys them and stops them from spreading. Think of it like popping a soap bubble — the alcohol disrupts the germ's protective layer so it cannot survive. It works quickly, usually within seconds of being applied to the skin.
common_side_effects: The most common side effects are dryness, irritation, or a mild burning sensation on the skin, especially with frequent use. Some people may notice redness or flaking skin with repeated application. Using a moisturizer regularly can help prevent dryness.
warnings: Do not swallow alcohol antiseptic — it is toxic if ingested and can cause serious harm. Keep it away from children, eyes, and open wounds or deep cuts. It is flammable, so keep away from flames or sparks while your hands are still wet with it. It does NOT remove all types of germs (like C. diff spores), so wash hands with soap and water when visibly dirty or after using the restroom.
typical_dosing: For hand sanitizer, apply a dime to quarter-sized amount to the palm of one hand. Rub your hands together, covering all surfaces including between fingers and the backs of hands, for about 20-30 seconds until dry. For skin prep before an injection, wipe the area with an alcohol pad in a circular motion and let it air dry for about 30 seconds before proceeding.
